---
title: "Tributary — Overview"
description: "A lead marketplace's business questions turned into decisions: which channels earn their spend, what duplicate consumers cost, where reserve floors sit, and whom to message."
---

## Four decisions

A simulated two-sided marketplace sells personal-loan leads to lenders
through a six-tier waterfall auction. Its data lives in three systems that
share no key, so the questions its executives would ask cannot be answered
from any one of them. Tributary builds that world, links its data with
measured accuracy, and then does the work the marketplace actually needs:

1. **Which channels earn their spend?** Paid ROAS runs from 0.94x
   (display, below break-even on $11.6M) to 3.06x (affiliate), and the
   click ranking the marketing team can compute alone inverts it.
   [Findings](dashboards.qmd)
2. **What do duplicate consumers cost?** 2.40M lead ids are 635,579
   people; buyers paid $12.0M (5.7% of revenue) for consumers they had
   bought within the prior 30 days. [Findings](dashboards.qmd)
3. **Where should reserve floors sit?** The level is right and the shape
   is wrong: reshaping the schedule lifts revenue per lead by +2.0% in
   counterfactual replay and +3.0% when the engine is re-run, about $4.2M a
   year at the logged volume. [Models](models.qmd), [memo](strategy-memo.qmd)
4. **Whom should we message?** One engagement segment carries the nurture
   effect; response-model targeting is worse than random; the pooled
   experiment is underpowered and says so. [Models](models.qmd)

Because the world is simulated from a hidden ground truth, every identity
claim underneath these numbers is scored, not asserted.

## From business problem to data science problem

The discipline this case study is meant to show is the translation step:
naming the decision, the metric, and the counterfactual before choosing a
method. The full table, with the data each row needed and its distance
from decision-grade, is in
[docs/problem_framing.md](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/docs/problem_framing.md).

| Business problem | Decision | Metric | Counterfactual | Method | Artifact | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Which channels earn their spend? | Next acquisition dollar; keep display? | ROAS, cost per sold lead | Marginal return, not average | Acquisition-cohort attribution through the auction | [Attribution](dashboards.qmd) | Answered; needs maturity adjustment and a spend test |
| What do duplicates cost? | Marketplace-side suppression or re-pricing | Revenue on re-sold consumers in a window | Same consumer, fresh | Identity resolution, windowed flags, sensitivity 1-90 days | [Identity](dashboards.qmd) | Answered; policy needs a buyer-response experiment |
| Where should floors sit? | Per-tier reserve schedule | Revenue per lead offered | Each logged lead under another schedule | Exact replay of logged bids, then engine re-run | [Model 3](models.qmd) | Decision-grade: validated, with a staged rollout in the [memo](strategy-memo.qmd) |
| Whom to message? | Send policy by segment | Incremental applications per contact | Randomized holdout | ITT read, cross-fitted T-learner on the action space | [Model 4](models.qmd) | Decision-grade as a ranking; follow-up test specified |
| What is a lead worth before its outcome exists? | Acquisition spend; what to do with unsold inventory | Expected revenue in dollars, censored leads included | Clearing at tiers never reached | Survival over the tier ladder; Tobit as a specification test | [Model 2](models.qmd) | Modeled; no decision yet consumes it |
| Which leads will sell? | None live: the auction answers it minutes later for free | Calibrated P(sold) | None needed | Calibrated gradient boosting, kept as the leakage and calibration contract | [Model 1](models.qmd) | Weakly motivated, and labelled so |
| Do sold leads fund? | Quality case for a stiffer tier-1 floor | Funded rate by price | Same lead at another price | Descriptive join | [Funnel](dashboards.qmd) | Direction only (calibrated) |
| How many consumers are there? | Every per-consumer figure | Precision, recall, purity | Hidden crosswalk | Probabilistic + deterministic linkage at stated operating points | [Identity modeling](silo-problem.qmd) | Answered and scored |

::: {.callout-note title="This page was rewritten after a correction"}
The first release of this case study led with the silo architecture and the cloud bill. After reading it start to finish, the author recorded that it read like data engineering and that the human-agent method was asserted rather than shown (intervention INT-017); the design document's tagline had been corrected on that point in the founding chat (INT-009), but its body and site plan had not, and the agents built to the body. The repositioning was run through the same harness as every other correction — a decision record (D14), a session log, and a rebuilt [method page](method.qmd) that renders the records instead of linking to them.
:::

## Results in sixty seconds

| Claim | Number | Where it's proven |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duplicate spend exposed | **$12.0M** (5.7% of revenue) paid for consumers bought within the prior 30 days; 635,579 consumers behind 2.40M lead ids (3.8x) | [Findings 1](dashboards.qmd) |
| Channel economics | ROAS **0.94x to 3.06x**; display below break-even; cost per sold lead $57 to $183 | [Findings 2](dashboards.qmd) |
| Reserve-floor policy | **+2.02%** revenue per lead in replay (95% CI +1.96% to +2.08%); **+2.98%** in the engine re-run (five-seed range +2.88% to +3.15%); zero if buyers give back 19% of the tier-1 increase | [Model 3](models.qmd), [memo](strategy-memo.qmd) |
| Send policy | Concentrated segment ranked first (+0.46pp predicted vs +0.52pp injected); response targeting **worse than random**; pooled test needs ~6.1M contacts, has 859k | [Model 4](models.qmd) |
| Lead valuation, censored half included | Top expected-value decile captures **33.3%** of revenue vs 14.7% for the table a team ships first; the textbook Tobit values unsold leads at $0.18 against $32.25 of logged demand | [Model 2](models.qmd) |
| Why you can trust these numbers | **95.3%** of auction events consumer-joinable (0% before); link F1 **0.879**, dedupe F1 **0.873**, purity 0.9998 against a hidden ground truth | [Identity modeling](silo-problem.qmd), [scorecard](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/er/scorecard.json) |

## What is here

All of it: the findings, the identity work, the four models, and the
strategy memo. The models were held off this site until their methodology
was reviewed and accepted (decision D11, 2026-09-02) and the floor policy's
uncertainty band until the method that produced it was ratified (D18), so
every number here has passed a review before being published rather than
after. That review is also why the models page opens the way it does: the
acceptance came with a pushback — what business problem is each model
actually solving — and answering it honestly demoted two of the four.

How the lab was built (three cloud silos, the simulator, and the one-cent
bill) is in the [appendix](cost.qmd); how the work was directed and
recorded is in [how this was built](method.qmd); the whole world regenerates
from one seeded command in [run it yourself](run-it.qmd).
